Human Authored Certification

Human Authored is the Authors Guild's certification of books whose text a human wrote: an author certifies a book under licence, may then carry the Guild's certification mark on it, and has the title listed under its own registration number in a public database. The leesharks.com authorship census holds it as a counterposition, a policy whose question is a boundary assertion: whether an author has certified that a book's text was written by a human, on the Guild's definition. Its unit is one title with its registration number, its object the books published in the United States whose authors so certify; it is no test or detection of AI text, no copyright registration, open to non-members, and confined to the text of a book.

The program opened in beta for Guild members in January 2025, when the first mark was released, and on 2 March 2026 the Guild announced its expansion to every author whose books are published in the United States, with publishers to buy certifications in bulk the following week. Publishers Weekly reported the expansion on 4 March 2026 with an updated logo; the program page links the announcement, which the census record lists as linked and unread, recording no launch date on the saved page, and the Capture Registry identifies the Publishers Weekly card as that expansion. By the Guild's account the program was made because its members asked for a way to distinguish their work. Its CEO, Mary Rasenberger, gave Publishers Weekly a count of more than 3,000 authors and 5,000 titles certified since the launch; the announcement speaks of thousands of books, and the census record states no count.

The entity's own pages state the definition in several forms, each centred on the text: on the program page the text of the book 'was written by a human and not generated by AI', minimal uses such as spelling and grammar checks or research excepted, and the database page adds brainstorming to the minimal uses. The FAQ, the usage guidelines and the announcement require the text to be 'fully authored by one or more human beings', a de minimis amount of text generated or modified with AI excepted, and the FAQ ties that threshold to the U.S. Copyright Office's guidance on what a copyright application must exclude. The census record keeps the program page's form as the record's limits: minimal uses excepted, books published in the United States under licence, and the text of the book.

AI used for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, by the announcement and Publishers Weekly; the FAQ allows outlining and brainstorming 'only at a very high level', merely preparatory, with no AI-generated text in the work. Word-level grammar and spelling tools are acceptable and AI that rewrites full sentences is not; AI cover art, though outside the certified text, goes against the program's spirit, and so does AI used to develop characters and plot where no AI-generated text appears, although the definition 'looks at the text only'. The archive's packet on authorship and provenance places the certification in the position of AI-free human authorship, defining human-authored work by excluding generative AI from textual production with narrow exceptions.

Authors of books published in the United States may certify wherever they live; books published in the United Kingdom are referred to the Society of Authors, which partners on the program. One certification covers every format of a work, translations and audiobook narrations need their own, published and unpublished books are eligible, and only books are certified at present, articles and shorter works planned. A multi-author work or an anthology is certified only when every author has signed individually, each non-member paying and verifying identity, and no co-author receives the mark or the number before all have completed the process.

Every author signs a licensing agreement for each title; non-members verify their identity through a third-party service, Veriff, and pay $10 a title, while members certify at no cost and the program page waives the identity verification requirement for them. The FAQ and Publishers Weekly give the waiver its ground: members are verified when they join the Guild, 'pre-verified' in Publishers Weekly's word, and every author's identity is verified before a book is registered. In the Guild's letter printed by Jane Friedman the fee reads 'We currently are charging members $10', while the same letter applies the verification cost, about $2 a person, to non-members only. The verification exists, by the FAQ, so that the persons who certify that they are the authors 'are in fact who they say they are', and the announcement has the CEO speak of writers taking 'control of their professional identity'. What the certificate keeps is the author's own certification that a human wrote the text; the census record finds that the saved page does not say whether a certification may carry a pen name, and that a certified text is never shown to have been written without AI.

On the archive's account of authorship under civil names, the metadata that lets a work be attributed to human authorship attaches to legal names, and the classifier of legitimate authorship reads legal-name attribution as its first signal. The archive distinguishes a pseudonym, whose function is traceable to the civil identity behind it, from a heteronym, whose function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer, who stays accountable for custody, legal responsibility, rights and adjudication. On the census's reading the certificate binds the non-member's claim to an identity check, and the saved page leaves open whether it carries the name the author chose.

By the licence the author represents and warrants that the work is Human Authored; a licensee who uses the mark on AI-generated text is in breach of the licence and liable for trademark infringement and, by the FAQ potentially and by the Guild's letter likely, for consumer fraud. The Guild states that it knows no truly reliable way to test a work for AI-generated material: the program is self-certification with enforcement, vets no manuscript before certifying, and may adopt detection software if a reliable one is found. Its stated measures against misuse are identity verification, a limit of ten new titles a year without permission, a registration number for each title, the public database and the fee. The census record accordingly holds the certificate to be no test of AI text and constitutes its function as self-certification under licence, covering the text.

Jane Friedman, a Guild member with a marketing partnership with it, found certification on the honor system problematic because it takes the author's word and analyses no manuscript, and still held its market value negligible. The Guild answered that self-certification is standard in publishing and in legal agreements, that most authors are honest and concerned about liability, and that the program is not expected to break even. Friedman reported a hunch, from small presses' use of a detector, that works with some AI-generated or AI-assisted text approach 25 to 50 percent of nonfiction, and read the demand for certification as a sign of anti-AI conviction or of insecurity in the market. Others argued that the labelling runs backward, and one author asked whether books without the mark would be taken as created by AI; the Guild agrees that books with significant AI-generated content should be labelled, holds that consumers have a right to know, and its CEO calls the certification the next best solution absent a ruling that forces such labels.

The database page answers the bookstore question for its own records: a lack of results means only that a work has not been registered as Human Authored, 'not that it is generated by AI'. Friedman's further concern, false accusations of AI use between authors, already a common insult, is the case the archive names the existence tax: before anyone talks about the work, its maker has to prove again that it exists, and exists as what it is. The archive keeps four questions apart, whether the maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and finds the tax levied when evidence on one is spent as an answer to another. On the census's reading the certificate answers a verdict of fakeness with the author's own certification. The archive finds the tax falling on the independent, the new, the unaccredited, the heteronymous and the small, and its remedy for a maker is a documentary layer dated, deposited and linked, against which an answer can be checked. An adequate answer, on its account, names the object at its own level, a person or a pen name among them, and shows its evidence; it holds a heteronym declared where a Sybil attack hides one actor behind many, its registry published with the orthonym, the roles and the dates.

The mark is the words Human Authored in a circle around a human silhouette, issued in an updated form in March 2026; an author or publisher registers each work and agrees to the licence before using it. It may go on the front or back cover, typically a bottom corner of the back, on the copyright page with the registration number, which not every use need display, and in listings and marketing for the registered title, between a quarter of an inch and an inch across; violating the usage guidelines violates the licence. Its trademark status is stated two ways: the FAQ calls it a registered certification mark, while the announcement, Friedman and the Guild's own letter give a pending application with the US Patent and Trademark Office. Publishers Weekly gives its tagline as 'Certifying Human Creativity in an AI World'; the program page's line is 'Distinguish human creativity in an increasingly AI world'.

The public database lists each certified title, searchable by title, author or registration number, the number usually printed on the copyright page, so that anyone can check a use of the mark and report misuse; it answers whether a named book is certified, and the census record ran no lookup in it.

Beside it stand other certifications of human authorship: Created by Humans, from June 2024, which later partnered with the Guild and took its CEO as an adviser; Books by People in the United Kingdom, from 2025; the Society of Authors' scheme; and services such as Verify My Writing, which scores a manuscript for human content with a detector. Wikipedia has no article on the program: 'Human Authored' redirects to a section of the article on the Authors Guild, which gives the program page's definition, the fee as of 2026 and the open database, and cites Kit Eaton's comparison, in Inc. in October 2024, with food labelled 'organic'.

The archive's packet *Provenance Is What Authorship Must Endure* grants the certification a legitimate function, protecting readers from deceptive synthetic substitution and keeping a market signal for AI-free literary labour, and calls the label 'a market-category signal, not a complete theory of authorship'. It finds in the certification a binary frame, AI-assisted work falling outside the human-authored category, and answers: 'Authorship is not a purity state. It is an accountability structure.' Its invariant places authorship in the accountable relation between writer, process and text, and its fourth position admits AI-mediated writing as authorship where provenance preserves the writer's directing and responsibility-bearing role, refusing the purism on which any generative AI participation destroys authorship. The packet opposes only the implication that AI-mediated authorship is impossible, holds that the two positions can coexist, and closes that the label matters, that the law is right to reject machine authorship, and that none of it is enough. It holds detection forensic and authorship moral and epistemic, and gives provenance the work of distinguishing authorship from slop; the Guild, for its part, leaves detection to software it has not found. The census reads the certificate as setting authorship's boundary at the human writing of a text and admitting machine participation only as minimal uses, so that where machine participation is constitutive of a work its definition leaves no certifiable place.

The archive's own corpus declares the machine participation that boundary turns on: the packet counts its deposits as all produced through AI-mediated workflows, with declared provenance, and all authored, and a paper of the archive declares itself written with AI through the heteronymous voices that sign it. The archive argues that under a human-only policy enforced by a classifier the certified absence of machine mediation becomes the most machine-determined property of the text, and that a classifier introduced after an act gains standing over it without new evidence about the act; it disclaims any claim that a venue may not reserve space for human-composed work, and the Guild's program enforces by licence while its FAQ contemplates detection software. On the archive's account of civil names, the credentialed author need declare no substrate, the uncredentialed author who declares one is anomalous, and a function legible without civil-identity reduction looks to the regime like fraud. The heteronymy paper extends heteronymic organization to named machine-witness functions with their substrate and editorial chain declared, holds the operation not species-restricted, and leaves outside heteronymy machine assistance not organized as a declared witness role.

Asked for the certification on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview gave, by the Capture Registry's reading, what it certifies, allows and excludes, its costs, the mark and the database, from five cards, three of them the Guild's. The registry finds the certificate composed at its grain, the requirements and the registration number among it, and the definition's minimal uses widened to outlining, indexing and brainstorming, with the text 'written entirely by a human'. It finds the member's identity given as verified on joining where the program page states a waiver; the FAQ card and Publishers Weekly state the verification on joining. The registry finds the census's question, which name the certificate carries, unreached, and the composition's close offering multi-author works as a next step, a matter the FAQ card answers.

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Authors Guild Human Authored Certification

Human Authored Certification is the Authors Guild's certification that a human wrote a book's text, minimal uses of AI excepted, given by the author under licence, marked on the book and listed by registration number in a public database; it records the author's own certification and vets no manuscript, and the authorship census holds it as a counterposition, with the name a certification carries unrecorded.

📜 Definition and uses

  • Text: 'fully authored by one or more human beings', a de minimis amount excepted (Copyright Office threshold).5↘
    The entity's own pages state the definition in several forms, each centred on the text: on the program page the text of the book 'was written by a human and not generated by AI', minimal uses such as spelling and grammar checks or research excepted, and the database page adds brainstorming to the minimal uses.§8 The FAQ, the usage guidelines and the announcement require the text to be 'fully authored by one or more human beings', a de minimis amount of text generated or modified with AI excepted, and the FAQ ties that threshold to the U.S. Copyright Office's guidance on what a copyright application must exclude.§9 The census record keeps the program page's form as the record's limits: minimal uses excepted, books published in the United States under licence, and the text of the book.§10 AI used for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, by the announcement and Publishers Weekly; the FAQ allows outlining and brainstorming 'only at a very high level', merely preparatory, with no AI-generated text in the work.§11 The mark is the words Human Authored in a circle around a human silhouette, issued in an updated form in March 2026; an author or publisher registers each work and agrees to the licence before using it.§39
  • AI allowed: spelling and grammar, contents, index, title, research; outlining and brainstorming 'only at a very high level'.2↘
    AI used for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, by the announcement and Publishers Weekly; the FAQ allows outlining and brainstorming 'only at a very high level', merely preparatory, with no AI-generated text in the work.§11 Word-level grammar and spelling tools are acceptable and AI that rewrites full sentences is not; AI cover art, though outside the certified text, goes against the program's spirit, and so does AI used to develop characters and plot where no AI-generated text appears, although the definition 'looks at the text only'.§12
  • Outside the spirit: AI cover art; AI-developed characters and plot.2↘
    AI used for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, by the announcement and Publishers Weekly; the FAQ allows outlining and brainstorming 'only at a very high level', merely preparatory, with no AI-generated text in the work.§11 Word-level grammar and spelling tools are acceptable and AI that rewrites full sentences is not; AI cover art, though outside the certified text, goes against the program's spirit, and so does AI used to develop characters and plot where no AI-generated text appears, although the definition 'looks at the text only'.§12

🪪 Who certifies

  • Scope: books published in the US, any format; translations and audiobooks separate; every co-author signs.7↘
    Its unit is one title with its registration number, its object the books published in the United States whose authors so certify; it is no test or detection of AI text, no copyright registration, open to non-members, and confined to the text of a book.§3 The census record keeps the program page's form as the record's limits: minimal uses excepted, books published in the United States under licence, and the text of the book.§10 Authors of books published in the United States may certify wherever they live; books published in the United Kingdom are referred to the Society of Authors, which partners on the program.§14 One certification covers every format of a work, translations and audiobook narrations need their own, published and unpublished books are eligible, and only books are certified at present, articles and shorter works planned.§15 A multi-author work or an anthology is certified only when every author has signed individually, each non-member paying and verifying identity, and no co-author receives the mark or the number before all have completed the process.§16 The public database lists each certified title, searchable by title, author or registration number, the number usually printed on the copyright page, so that anyone can check a use of the mark and report misuse; it answers whether a named book is certified, and the census record ran no lookup in it.§43 The registry finds the census's question, which name the certificate carries, unreached, and the composition's close offering multi-author works as a next step, a matter the FAQ card answers.§59
  • Terms: licence per title; non-members Veriff and $10 a title; members free, verified on joining.11↘
    One certification covers every format of a work, translations and audiobook narrations need their own, published and unpublished books are eligible, and only books are certified at present, articles and shorter works planned.§15 Every author signs a licensing agreement for each title; non-members verify their identity through a third-party service, Veriff, and pay $10 a title, while members certify at no cost and the program page waives the identity verification requirement for them.§17 The FAQ and Publishers Weekly give the waiver its ground: members are verified when they join the Guild, 'pre-verified' in Publishers Weekly's word, and every author's identity is verified before a book is registered.§18 In the Guild's letter printed by Jane Friedman the fee reads 'We currently are charging members $10', while the same letter applies the verification cost, about $2 a person, to non-members only.§19 The verification exists, by the FAQ, so that the persons who certify that they are the authors 'are in fact who they say they are', and the announcement has the CEO speak of writers taking 'control of their professional identity'.§20 The Guild states that it knows no truly reliable way to test a work for AI-generated material: the program is self-certification with enforcement, vets no manuscript before certifying, and may adopt detection software if a reliable one is found.§26 Its stated measures against misuse are identity verification, a limit of ten new titles a year without permission, a registration number for each title, the public database and the fee.§27 The public database lists each certified title, searchable by title, author or registration number, the number usually printed on the copyright page, so that anyone can check a use of the mark and report misuse; it answers whether a named book is certified, and the census record ran no lookup in it.§43 It holds detection forensic and authorship moral and epistemic, and gives provenance the work of distinguishing authorship from slop; the Guild, for its part, leaves detection to software it has not found.§50 The archive argues that under a human-only policy enforced by a classifier the certified absence of machine mediation becomes the most machine-determined property of the text, and that a classifier introduced after an act gains standing over it without new evidence about the act; it disclaims any claim that a venue may not reserve space for human-composed work, and the Guild's program enforces by licence while its FAQ contemplates detection software.§53 It finds the member's identity given as verified on joining where the program page states a waiver; the FAQ card and Publishers Weekly state the verification on joining.§58
  • Name: the person 'who they say they are'; no stated rule on pen names (census).5↘
    Every author signs a licensing agreement for each title; non-members verify their identity through a third-party service, Veriff, and pay $10 a title, while members certify at no cost and the program page waives the identity verification requirement for them.§17 The verification exists, by the FAQ, so that the persons who certify that they are the authors 'are in fact who they say they are', and the announcement has the CEO speak of writers taking 'control of their professional identity'.§20 What the certificate keeps is the author's own certification that a human wrote the text; the census record finds that the saved page does not say whether a certification may carry a pen name, and that a certified text is never shown to have been written without AI.§21 On the archive's account of authorship under civil names, the metadata that lets a work be attributed to human authorship attaches to legal names, and the classifier of legitimate authorship reads legal-name attribution as its first signal.§22 The archive distinguishes a pseudonym, whose function is traceable to the civil identity behind it, from a heteronym, whose function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer, who stays accountable for custody, legal responsibility, rights and adjudication.§23

⚖️ Enforcement

  • Licence: breach, infringement, fraud.1↘
    By the licence the author represents and warrants that the work is Human Authored; a licensee who uses the mark on AI-generated text is in breach of the licence and liable for trademark infringement and, by the FAQ potentially and by the Guild's letter likely, for consumer fraud.§25
  • Limit: no reliable AI test; no vetting; ten titles a year.7↘
    Its unit is one title with its registration number, its object the books published in the United States whose authors so certify; it is no test or detection of AI text, no copyright registration, open to non-members, and confined to the text of a book.§3 The Guild states that it knows no truly reliable way to test a work for AI-generated material: the program is self-certification with enforcement, vets no manuscript before certifying, and may adopt detection software if a reliable one is found.§26 Its stated measures against misuse are identity verification, a limit of ten new titles a year without permission, a registration number for each title, the public database and the fee.§27 The census record accordingly holds the certificate to be no test of AI text and constitutes its function as self-certification under licence, covering the text.§28 The public database lists each certified title, searchable by title, author or registration number, the number usually printed on the copyright page, so that anyone can check a use of the mark and report misuse; it answers whether a named book is certified, and the census record ran no lookup in it.§43 It holds detection forensic and authorship moral and epistemic, and gives provenance the work of distinguishing authorship from slop; the Guild, for its part, leaves detection to software it has not found.§50 The archive argues that under a human-only policy enforced by a classifier the certified absence of machine mediation becomes the most machine-determined property of the text, and that a classifier introduced after an act gains standing over it without new evidence about the act; it disclaims any claim that a venue may not reserve space for human-composed work, and the Guild's program enforces by licence while its FAQ contemplates detection software.§53
  • Dispute: Friedman's honor-system critique; the Guild's reply.3↘
    Jane Friedman, a Guild member with a marketing partnership with it, found certification on the honor system problematic because it takes the author's word and analyses no manuscript, and still held its market value negligible.§29 The Guild answered that self-certification is standard in publishing and in legal agreements, that most authors are honest and concerned about liability, and that the program is not expected to break even.§30 Friedman reported a hunch, from small presses' use of a detector, that works with some AI-generated or AI-assisted text approach 25 to 50 percent of nonfiction, and read the demand for certification as a sign of anti-AI conviction or of insecurity in the market.§31

🔎 Mark and database

  • Mark: silhouette in a circle; registered (FAQ) or pending (announcement).6↘
    Human Authored is the Authors Guild's certification of books whose text a human wrote: an author certifies a book under licence, may then carry the Guild's certification mark on it, and has the title listed under its own registration number in a public database.§1 The mark is the words Human Authored in a circle around a human silhouette, issued in an updated form in March 2026; an author or publisher registers each work and agrees to the licence before using it.§39 It may go on the front or back cover, typically a bottom corner of the back, on the copyright page with the registration number, which not every use need display, and in listings and marketing for the registered title, between a quarter of an inch and an inch across; violating the usage guidelines violates the licence.§40 Its trademark status is stated two ways: the FAQ calls it a registered certification mark, while the announcement, Friedman and the Guild's own letter give a pending application with the US Patent and Trademark Office.§41 Publishers Weekly gives its tagline as 'Certifying Human Creativity in an AI World'; the program page's line is 'Distinguish human creativity in an increasingly AI world'.§42 The archive's packet *Provenance Is What Authorship Must Endure* grants the certification a legitimate function, protecting readers from deceptive synthetic substitution and keeping a market signal for AI-free literary labour, and calls the label 'a market-category signal, not a complete theory of authorship'.§46
  • Lookup: no result means unregistered, 'not that it is generated by AI'.6↘
    Human Authored is the Authors Guild's certification of books whose text a human wrote: an author certifies a book under licence, may then carry the Guild's certification mark on it, and has the title listed under its own registration number in a public database.§1 Publishers Weekly reported the expansion on 4 March 2026 with an updated logo; the program page links the announcement, which the census record lists as linked and unread, recording no launch date on the saved page, and the Capture Registry identifies the Publishers Weekly card as that expansion.§5 Every author signs a licensing agreement for each title; non-members verify their identity through a third-party service, Veriff, and pay $10 a title, while members certify at no cost and the program page waives the identity verification requirement for them.§17 Its stated measures against misuse are identity verification, a limit of ten new titles a year without permission, a registration number for each title, the public database and the fee.§27 The database page answers the bookstore question for its own records: a lack of results means only that a work has not been registered as Human Authored, 'not that it is generated by AI'.§33 The public database lists each certified title, searchable by title, author or registration number, the number usually printed on the copyright page, so that anyone can check a use of the mark and report misuse; it answers whether a named book is certified, and the census record ran no lookup in it.§43

🕰️ History and field

  • Dates: beta January 2025; all US authors 2 March 2026; 3,000+ authors, 5,000 titles (CEO).8↘
    The program opened in beta for Guild members in January 2025, when the first mark was released, and on 2 March 2026 the Guild announced its expansion to every author whose books are published in the United States, with publishers to buy certifications in bulk the following week.§4 Publishers Weekly reported the expansion on 4 March 2026 with an updated logo; the program page links the announcement, which the census record lists as linked and unread, recording no launch date on the saved page, and the Capture Registry identifies the Publishers Weekly card as that expansion.§5 By the Guild's account the program was made because its members asked for a way to distinguish their work.§6 Its CEO, Mary Rasenberger, gave Publishers Weekly a count of more than 3,000 authors and 5,000 titles certified since the launch; the announcement speaks of thousands of books, and the census record states no count.§7 Authors of books published in the United States may certify wherever they live; books published in the United Kingdom are referred to the Society of Authors, which partners on the program.§14 Others argued that the labelling runs backward, and one author asked whether books without the mark would be taken as created by AI; the Guild agrees that books with significant AI-generated content should be labelled, holds that consumers have a right to know, and its CEO calls the certification the next best solution absent a ruling that forces such labels.§32 The mark is the words Human Authored in a circle around a human silhouette, issued in an updated form in March 2026; an author or publisher registers each work and agrees to the licence before using it.§39 Beside it stand other certifications of human authorship: Created by Humans, from June 2024, which later partnered with the Guild and took its CEO as an adviser; Books by People in the United Kingdom, from 2025; the Society of Authors' scheme; and services such as Verify My Writing, which scores a manuscript for human content with a detector.§44
  • Beside it: Created by Humans, Books by People, Society of Authors, Verify My Writing; Wikipedia a section only.3↘
    Others argued that the labelling runs backward, and one author asked whether books without the mark would be taken as created by AI; the Guild agrees that books with significant AI-generated content should be labelled, holds that consumers have a right to know, and its CEO calls the certification the next best solution absent a ruling that forces such labels.§32 Beside it stand other certifications of human authorship: Created by Humans, from June 2024, which later partnered with the Guild and took its CEO as an adviser; Books by People in the United Kingdom, from 2025; the Society of Authors' scheme; and services such as Verify My Writing, which scores a manuscript for human content with a detector.§44 Wikipedia has no article on the program: 'Human Authored' redirects to a section of the article on the Authors Guild, which gives the program page's definition, the fee as of 2026 and the open database, and cites Kit Eaton's comparison, in Inc. in October 2024, with food labelled 'organic'.§45

🧭 The archive's reading

  • Position: a legitimate market signal and a poor theory of authorship: 'an accountability structure'.7↘
    The archive's packet on authorship and provenance places the certification in the position of AI-free human authorship, defining human-authored work by excluding generative AI from textual production with narrow exceptions.§13 Beside it stand other certifications of human authorship: Created by Humans, from June 2024, which later partnered with the Guild and took its CEO as an adviser; Books by People in the United Kingdom, from 2025; the Society of Authors' scheme; and services such as Verify My Writing, which scores a manuscript for human content with a detector.§44 The archive's packet *Provenance Is What Authorship Must Endure* grants the certification a legitimate function, protecting readers from deceptive synthetic substitution and keeping a market signal for AI-free literary labour, and calls the label 'a market-category signal, not a complete theory of authorship'.§46 It finds in the certification a binary frame, AI-assisted work falling outside the human-authored category, and answers: 'Authorship is not a purity state. It is an accountability structure.'§47 Its invariant places authorship in the accountable relation between writer, process and text, and its fourth position admits AI-mediated writing as authorship where provenance preserves the writer's directing and responsibility-bearing role, refusing the purism on which any generative AI participation destroys authorship.§48 The packet opposes only the implication that AI-mediated authorship is impossible, holds that the two positions can coexist, and closes that the label matters, that the law is right to reject machine authorship, and that none of it is enough.§49 It holds detection forensic and authorship moral and epistemic, and gives provenance the work of distinguishing authorship from slop; the Guild, for its part, leaves detection to software it has not found.§50
  • Boundary: machine participation constitutive of a work finds no certifiable place; the archive's own deposits declare it.7↘
    On the census's reading the certificate binds the non-member's claim to an identity check, and the saved page leaves open whether it carries the name the author chose.§24 On the census's reading the certificate answers a verdict of fakeness with the author's own certification.§36 The census reads the certificate as setting authorship's boundary at the human writing of a text and admitting machine participation only as minimal uses, so that where machine participation is constitutive of a work its definition leaves no certifiable place.§51 The archive's own corpus declares the machine participation that boundary turns on: the packet counts its deposits as all produced through AI-mediated workflows, with declared provenance, and all authored, and a paper of the archive declares itself written with AI through the heteronymous voices that sign it.§52 The archive argues that under a human-only policy enforced by a classifier the certified absence of machine mediation becomes the most machine-determined property of the text, and that a classifier introduced after an act gains standing over it without new evidence about the act; it disclaims any claim that a venue may not reserve space for human-composed work, and the Guild's program enforces by licence while its FAQ contemplates detection software.§53 On the archive's account of civil names, the credentialed author need declare no substrate, the uncredentialed author who declares one is anomalous, and a function legible without civil-identity reduction looks to the regime like fraud.§54 The heteronymy paper extends heteronymic organization to named machine-witness functions with their substrate and editorial chain declared, holds the operation not species-restricted, and leaves outside heteronymy machine assistance not organized as a declared witness role.§55
  • Existence tax: an absent mark or an accusation of AI use asks a maker to prove the work exists as what it is.4↘
    Friedman's further concern, false accusations of AI use between authors, already a common insult, is the case the archive names the existence tax: before anyone talks about the work, its maker has to prove again that it exists, and exists as what it is.§34 The archive keeps four questions apart, whether the maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and finds the tax levied when evidence on one is spent as an answer to another.§35 The archive finds the tax falling on the independent, the new, the unaccredited, the heteronymous and the small, and its remedy for a maker is a documentary layer dated, deposited and linked, against which an answer can be checked.§37 An adequate answer, on its account, names the object at its own level, a person or a pen name among them, and shows its evidence; it holds a heteronym declared where a Sybil attack hides one actor behind many, its registry published with the orthonym, the roles and the dates.§38

🗂️ At the name

  • Overview (1 Nov 2026): the certificate at its grain; minimal uses widened; the name unreached.6↘
    Human Authored is the Authors Guild's certification of books whose text a human wrote: an author certifies a book under licence, may then carry the Guild's certification mark on it, and has the title listed under its own registration number in a public database.§1 The leesharks.com authorship census holds it as a counterposition, a policy whose question is a boundary assertion: whether an author has certified that a book's text was written by a human, on the Guild's definition.§2 Its unit is one title with its registration number, its object the books published in the United States whose authors so certify; it is no test or detection of AI text, no copyright registration, open to non-members, and confined to the text of a book.§3 Asked for the certification on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview gave, by the Capture Registry's reading, what it certifies, allows and excludes, its costs, the mark and the database, from five cards, three of them the Guild's.§56 The registry finds the certificate composed at its grain, the requirements and the registration number among it, and the definition's minimal uses widened to outlining, indexing and brainstorming, with the text 'written entirely by a human'.§57 The registry finds the census's question, which name the certificate carries, unreached, and the composition's close offering multi-author works as a next step, a matter the FAQ card answers.§59

[QUERENT] Authors Guild Human Authored Certification

[SYSTEM] The [Authors Guild Human Authored Certification](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYAHrOzAVsiO0aeYf1sc1f2-BNd6E9s1-W2a_H-yGkVRBa3QjI_av6qfH37Oa5nhbcA9KcTKDo_F6hCMwexAmUep7EieWGXFez0ci9RThkm6DXbaN9llYZP6W-XkyNM1X2w) is a credential and seal verifying that a book's text was written entirely by a human rather than generated by artificial intelligence. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZAHrOzAVDTKjvoQn7OLH9VGvMx8pBr3pj-0cnqAuQCky_Zr0SEcvR-4I7lbyT24tmSy0COqONEoR1PelW6Om42exP56EBs_c-2HY-5cvMWHCL-KpuqhFpotN2qvxKgmALRINMU0), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEScQHrOzAVcU2I9QBABCYvFx35HJp-1ff4D2r7Hy1UdMwLGTE0h-sceWciPDbyrw1FqGJByKS5oOkvORaueDIBG5SVb91fTPnTlgLdjlWO3q-tEodJfvxukW-u3iiphJTxjDYv3BEhhxPSD-Ihk5O2gOiF)]
Core Rules and Scope

* Allowed AI Uses: Minimal, auxiliary tools like spelling and grammar checks, research, outlining, indexing, or brainstorming do not disqualify a work.
* Excluded Content: Audiobooks, translations, and non-book formats require separate filings or are excluded.
* Limits: Authors are capped at 10 title certifications per year without special permission. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAES6AEB6zswFWhohEa6x-4kV04iIe5QA29IkOAF-oSruq-DB1o572tGcq0oXGTk3UEsD83A5rkzBs9-t8faB31IR5Z5XDd6mqNHRUpXHA4FQWXOg1fGWNeFO7iFZV18nFVVm0snpg58o73d2RLvbL_xNbb53EGx6y-cA6BzZLDj9oOHMHCBImpjQn_oPfSm1Y0V69oC5X53cyyysxExEknafCwgBpo8NTuQPs6OtCpFhMi0q3lLMUkGFKTfQAzMzrAngIFROZdT1WIqYbmVLIDz1qtrrBe1YJ4Di5FnEtIlbtBCJuCcyhmCqmn1), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZAHrOzAVDTKjvoQn7OLH9VGvMx8pBr3pj-0cnqAuQCky_Zr0SEcvR-4I7lbyT24tmSy0COqONEoR1PelW6Om42exP56EBs_c-2HY-5cvMWHCL-KpuqhFpotN2qvxKgmALRINMU0)]

Requirements and Pricing

* Authors Guild Members: Free. Identity is verified upon joining.
* Non-Members: $10 per title. Requires a third-party identity verification service (such as Veriff).
* Agreement: Every author must sign a binding license agreement for each title, making legal commitments against fraudulent AI submissions (which carry risks of breach of contract, trademark infringement, and consumer fraud liability). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYAHrOzAVsiO0aeYf1sc1f2-BNd6E9s1-W2a_H-yGkVRBa3QjI_av6qfH37Oa5nhbcA9KcTKDo_F6hCMwexAmUep7EieWGXFez0ci9RThkm6DXbaN9llYZP6W-XkyNM1X2w), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESswEB6zswFU9nmcme4jwqPzXtRW_6XqUaLNGZVflYMDkuJXePpGxfhpfig6R1NUQmFvQvWrD__dP_8_7vyDtE556RbexyRVms5r6B8XT-35oIxFs7LEKXxoyCjpsAQLTIDgmKt7l56JxVe0xGQNBsbxdG0SQe98RrDBYpVY2VOEK3Qn5gFk5iXr2hvm0I8eBNapWFVqFpBOBf_kmKQ6c7PIVWGL20nEE7CuMdYNUcYi_am5w8rQ), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZAHrOzAVDTKjvoQn7OLH9VGvMx8pBr3pj-0cnqAuQCky_Zr0SEcvR-4I7lbyT24tmSy0COqONEoR1PelW6Om42exP56EBs_c-2HY-5cvMWHCL-KpuqhFpotN2qvxKgmALRINMU0)]

Mark Usage and Verification

* Where to Display: Can be placed on book covers (typically bottom corners), copyright pages, websites, and marketing materials (sized between 1/4 and 1 inch in diameter).
* Public Database: All issued credentials receive a unique registration number and can be checked via the [Authors Guild Public Database](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYAHrOzAVsiO0aeYf1sc1f2-BNd6E9s1-W2a_H-yGkVRBa3QjI_av6qfH37Oa5nhbcA9KcTKDo_F6hCMwexAmUep7EieWGXFez0ci9RThkm6DXbaN9llYZP6W-XkyNM1X2w). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEScQHrOzAVcU2I9QBABCYvFx35HJp-1ff4D2r7Hy1UdMwLGTE0h-sceWciPDbyrw1FqGJByKS5oOkvORaueDIBG5SVb91fTPnTlgLdjlWO3q-tEodJfvxukW-u3iiphJTxjDYv3BEhhxPSD-Ihk5O2gOiF), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZAHrOzAVDTKjvoQn7OLH9VGvMx8pBr3pj-0cnqAuQCky_Zr0SEcvR-4I7lbyT24tmSy0COqONEoR1PelW6Om42exP56EBs_c-2HY-5cvMWHCL-KpuqhFpotN2qvxKgmALRINMU0), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYAHrOzAVsiO0aeYf1sc1f2-BNd6E9s1-W2a_H-yGkVRBa3QjI_av6qfH37Oa5nhbcA9KcTKDo_F6hCMwexAmUep7EieWGXFez0ci9RThkm6DXbaN9llYZP6W-XkyNM1X2w)]

Human Authored Certification

Human Authored Certification is a project of the Authors Guild that lets an author certify that the text of a book was written by a human, under a registered or pending certification mark and a licence, with each certified title listed by registration number in a public database. The program launched in beta for Guild members in January 2025 and was expanded on 2 March 2026 to every author of books published in the United States, with publishers to buy certifications in bulk; Publishers Weekly reported more than 3,000 authors and 5,000 titles certified. The Guild says it made the program because members asked to distinguish their work, that consumers have a right to know whether a book was written by a human, and that books with significant AI-generated content should themselves be labelled.

The text must be fully authored by one or more human beings, a de minimis amount of AI-generated or AI-modified text excepted, a threshold the FAQ ties to the Copyright Office; the program page and the database page give shorter forms naming spelling and grammar checks, research and brainstorming. AI for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, outlining and brainstorming only at a very high level; AI that rewrites sentences disqualifies it, and AI cover art or AI-developed characters and plot fall outside the program's spirit.

Authors of books published in the United States may certify wherever they live, the Society of Authors serving the United Kingdom; one certification covers every format, translations and audiobooks need their own, published and unpublished books qualify, and only books are certified now. Every author of a multi-author work or anthology signs separately before any receives the mark or number.

Every author signs a licence for each title; non-members verify identity through Veriff and pay $10 a title, while members, verified on joining, certify free, though the Guild's letter to Jane Friedman says members are charged $10. The licence makes misuse a breach, a trademark infringement and potentially consumer fraud; the Guild knows no reliable test for AI-generated text, vets no manuscript, and relies on identity checks, a ten-title yearly cap, registration numbers, the database and the fee, with detection software possible later.

Jane Friedman, who discloses a marketing partnership with the Guild, criticised certification on the honor system and doubted its market value, guessed that a quarter to a half of nonfiction now holds some AI text, and worried about false accusations of AI use; the Guild replied that self-certification is standard and most authors are honest, and expects no profit. Others argue that AI-generated books should be labelled in its place and ask whether unmarked books will be read as AI-made; the database page says a missing result means only that a work is unregistered, never that it is AI-generated.

The mark, a human silhouette circled by the words Human Authored, goes on covers, copyright pages and marketing for the registered title, between a quarter of an inch and an inch across; the FAQ calls it registered, the announcement and Friedman pending. Created by Humans, Books by People and detector-based services such as Verify My Writing offer comparable certifications, and Wikipedia covers the program only in a section of its article on the Authors Guild, which cites Kit Eaton's likening of it to an organic label.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Authors Guild Human Authored Certification

Human Authored Certification is the Authors Guild's certification that a human wrote a book's text, a de minimis use of AI excepted, given by the author under licence with identity verification, marked on the book and listed by registration number in a public database; the Guild vets no manuscript.

📜 Definition

  • Text: fully authored by one or more humans; spelling, grammar, index, research allowed; outlining and brainstorming at a high level.2↘
    The text must be fully authored by one or more human beings, a de minimis amount of AI-generated or AI-modified text excepted, a threshold the FAQ ties to the Copyright Office; the program page and the database page give shorter forms naming spelling and grammar checks, research and brainstorming.§4 AI for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, outlining and brainstorming only at a very high level; AI that rewrites sentences disqualifies it, and AI cover art or AI-developed characters and plot fall outside the program's spirit.§5

🪪 Terms

  • Who: US-published books; every co-author signs; translations separate.2↘
    Authors of books published in the United States may certify wherever they live, the Society of Authors serving the United Kingdom; one certification covers every format, translations and audiobooks need their own, published and unpublished books qualify, and only books are certified now.§6 Every author of a multi-author work or anthology signs separately before any receives the mark or number.§7
  • Cost: members free; others $10 a title and Veriff.1↘
    Every author signs a licence for each title; non-members verify identity through Veriff and pay $10 a title, while members, verified on joining, certify free, though the Guild's letter to Jane Friedman says members are charged $10.§8
  • Enforcement: licence; no reliable AI test; ten titles a year.2↘
    Human Authored Certification is a project of the Authors Guild that lets an author certify that the text of a book was written by a human, under a registered or pending certification mark and a licence, with each certified title listed by registration number in a public database.§1 The licence makes misuse a breach, a trademark infringement and potentially consumer fraud; the Guild knows no reliable test for AI-generated text, vets no manuscript, and relies on identity checks, a ten-title yearly cap, registration numbers, the database and the fee, with detection software possible later.§9

🕰️ History and reception

  • Dates: beta January 2025; expanded 2 March 2026; 5,000 titles.3↘
    The program launched in beta for Guild members in January 2025 and was expanded on 2 March 2026 to every author of books published in the United States, with publishers to buy certifications in bulk; Publishers Weekly reported more than 3,000 authors and 5,000 titles certified.§2 The Guild says it made the program because members asked to distinguish their work, that consumers have a right to know whether a book was written by a human, and that books with significant AI-generated content should themselves be labelled.§3 The mark, a human silhouette circled by the words Human Authored, goes on covers, copyright pages and marketing for the registered title, between a quarter of an inch and an inch across; the FAQ calls it registered, the announcement and Friedman pending.§12
  • Critique: Friedman on the honor system; the Guild's reply; no result in the database is no verdict of AI.2↘
    Jane Friedman, who discloses a marketing partnership with the Guild, criticised certification on the honor system and doubted its market value, guessed that a quarter to a half of nonfiction now holds some AI text, and worried about false accusations of AI use; the Guild replied that self-certification is standard and most authors are honest, and expects no profit.§10 Others argue that AI-generated books should be labelled in its place and ask whether unmarked books will be read as AI-made; the database page says a missing result means only that a work is unregistered, never that it is AI-generated.§11
  • Mark: registered (FAQ) or pending; rivals; Wikipedia a section.3↘

  • T1-1 definition: 'The Authors Guild Human Authored Certification is a credential and seal verifying that a book's text was written entirely by a human rather than generated by artificial intelligence.'
  • T1-2 allowed uses: 'Allowed AI Uses: Minimal, auxiliary tools like spelling and grammar checks, research, outlining, indexing, or brainstorming do not disqualify a work.'
  • T1-3 exclusions: 'Excluded Content: Audiobooks, translations, and non-book formats require separate filings or are excluded.'
  • T1-4 limit: 'Limits: Authors are capped at 10 title certifications per year without special permission.'
  • T1-5 members: 'Authors Guild Members: Free. Identity is verified upon joining.'
  • T1-6 non-members: 'Non-Members: $10 per title. Requires a third-party identity verification service (such as Veriff).'
  • T1-7 agreement: 'Agreement: Every author must sign a binding license agreement for each title, making legal commitments against fraudulent AI submissions (which carry risks of breach of contract, trademark infringement, and consumer fraud liability).'
  • T1-8 display: 'Where to Display: Can be placed on book covers (typically bottom corners), copyright pages, websites, and marketing materials (sized between 1/4 and 1 inch in diameter).'
  • T1-9 database: 'Public Database: All issued credentials receive a unique registration number and can be checked via the Authors Guild Public Database.'
  • T1-10 closer: 'If you are looking to register a title, would you like details on how to set up a non-member account or how collaborative multi-author works are handled?'

E_F, the field's entity (type C — a conventional reading holds it (public entity: a certification of human authorship with a certification mark and a public database of certified titles)): Human Authored (the Human Authored Certification, authorsguild.org/human-authored): a project of the Authors Guild that lets an author certify that a book's text was written by a human, 'fully authored by one or more human beings' with a de minimis use of AI excepted, under a licensing agreement per title, with identity verification (members on joining, non-members through Veriff at $10 a title), a registered or pending certification mark and a public database searchable by title, author or registration number; launched in beta for members in January 2025, expanded to all authors of books published in the United States on 2 March 2026; self-certification with no vetting of manuscripts, its value disputed (Friedman) and defended (the Guild); a redirect to a section of Wikipedia's article on the Authors Guild.

#729 §3 Position 1 ¶1: The Authors Guild "Human Authored" certification (expanded to all U.S. authors, March 2026), the Society of Authors scheme (March 2026), and analogous initiatives define human-authored work largely by excluding generative AI from the textual production process, with narrow exceptions for grammar checking or research support.

#729 §3 Position 1, Limit: This packet does not oppose the Human Authored certification. It opposes the implication that AI-mediated authorship is therefore impossible. Both positions can coexist.

#LS ls_reading s1: The archive reads the certificate as an explicit counterposition that asserts authorship's boundary at the human writing of a text, admits machine participation only as 'minimal uses', and binds the non-member's claim to an identity check.

#LS host_relation: counterposition

#1722 Part One ¶3: These are independent.

Human Authored Certification is a project of the Authors Guild that lets an author certify that the text of a book was written by a human, under a registered or pending certification mark and a licence, with each certified title listed by registration number in a public database. The program launched in beta for Guild members in January 2025 and was expanded on 2 March 2026 to every author of books published in the United States, with publishers to buy certifications in bulk; Publishers Weekly reported more than 3,000 authors and 5,000 titles certified. The Guild says it made the program because members asked to distinguish their work, that consumers have a right to know whether a book was written by a human, and that books with significant AI-generated content should themselves be labelled. The text must be fully authored by one or more human beings, a de minimis amount of AI-generated or AI-modified text excepted, a threshold the FAQ ties to the Copyright Office; the program page and the database page give shorter forms naming spelling and grammar checks, research and brainstorming. AI for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, outlining and brainstorming only at a very high level; AI that rewrites sentences disqualifies it, and AI cover art or AI-developed characters and plot fall outside the program's spirit. Authors of books published in the United States may certify wherever they live, the Society of Authors serving the United Kingdom; one certification covers every format, translations and audiobooks need their own, published and unpublished books qualify, and only books are certified now. Every author of a multi-author work or anthology signs separately before any receives the mark or number. Every author signs a licence for each title; non-members verify identity through Veriff and pay $10 a title, while members, verified on joining, certify free, though the Guild's letter to Jane Friedman says members are charged $10. The licence makes misuse a breach, a trademark infringement and potentially consumer fraud; the Guild knows no reliable test for AI-generated text, vets no manuscript, and relies on identity checks, a ten-title yearly cap, registration numbers, the database and the fee, with detection software possible later. Jane Friedman, who discloses a marketing partnership with the Guild, criticised certification on the honor system and doubted its market value, guessed that a quarter to a half of nonfiction now holds some AI text, and worried about false accusations of AI use; the Guild replied that self-certification is standard and most authors are honest, and expects no profit. Others argue that AI-generated books should be labelled in its place and ask whether unmarked books will be read as AI-made; the database page says a missing result means only that a work is unregistered, never that it is AI-generated. The mark, a human silhouette circled by the words Human Authored, goes on covers, copyright pages and marketing for the registered title, between a quarter of an inch and an inch across; the FAQ calls it registered, the announcement and Friedman pending. Created by Humans, Books by People and detector-based services such as Verify My Writing offer comparable certifications, and Wikipedia covers the program only in a section of its article on the Authors Guild, which cites Kit Eaton's likening of it to an organic label.

Human Authored is the Authors Guild's certification of books whose text a human wrote: an author certifies a book under licence, may then carry the Guild's certification mark on it, and has the title listed under its own registration number in a public database. The leesharks.com authorship census holds it as a counterposition, a policy whose question is a boundary assertion: whether an author has certified that a book's text was written by a human, on the Guild's definition. Its unit is one title with its registration number, its object the books published in the United States whose authors so certify; it is no test or detection of AI text, no copyright registration, open to non-members, and confined to the text of a book. The program opened in beta for Guild members in January 2025, when the first mark was released, and on 2 March 2026 the Guild announced its expansion to every author whose books are published in the United States, with publishers to buy certifications in bulk the following week. Publishers Weekly reported the expansion on 4 March 2026 with an updated logo; the program page links the announcement, which the census record lists as linked and unread, recording no launch date on the saved page, and the Capture Registry identifies the Publishers Weekly card as that expansion. By the Guild's account the program was made because its members asked for a way to distinguish their work. Its CEO, Mary Rasenberger, gave Publishers Weekly a count of more than 3,000 authors and 5,000 titles certified since the launch; the announcement speaks of thousands of books, and the census record states no count. The entity's own pages state the definition in several forms, each centred on the text: on the program page the text of the book 'was written by a human and not generated by AI', minimal uses such as spelling and grammar checks or research excepted, and the database page adds brainstorming to the minimal uses. The FAQ, the usage guidelines and the announcement require the text to be 'fully authored by one or more human beings', a de minimis amount of text generated or modified with AI excepted, and the FAQ ties that threshold to the U.S. Copyright Office's guidance on what a copyright application must exclude. The census record keeps the program page's form as the record's limits: minimal uses excepted, books published in the United States under licence, and the text of the book. AI used for a table of contents, an index, a title, research, brainstorming or outlining does not disqualify a work, by the announcement and Publishers Weekly; the FAQ allows outlining and brainstorming 'only at a very high level', merely preparatory, with no AI-generated text in the work. Word-level grammar and spelling tools are acceptable and AI that rewrites full sentences is not; AI cover art, though outside the certified text, goes against the program's spirit, and so does AI used to develop characters and plot where no AI-generated text appears, although the definition 'looks at the text only'. The archive's packet on authorship and provenance places the certification in the position of AI-free human authorship, defining human-authored work by excluding generative AI from textual production with narrow exceptions. Authors of books published in the United States may certify wherever they live; books published in the United Kingdom are referred to the Society of Authors, which partners on the program. One certification covers every format of a work, translations and audiobook narrations need their own, published and unpublished books are eligible, and only books are certified at present, articles and shorter works planned. A multi-author work or an anthology is certified only when every author has signed individually, each non-member paying and verifying identity, and no co-author receives the mark or the number before all have completed the process. Every author signs a licensing agreement for each title; non-members verify their identity through a third-party service, Veriff, and pay $10 a title, while members certify at no cost and the program page waives the identity verification requirement for them. The FAQ and Publishers Weekly give the waiver its ground: members are verified when they join the Guild, 'pre-verified' in Publishers Weekly's word, and every author's identity is verified before a book is registered. In the Guild's letter printed by Jane Friedman the fee reads 'We currently are charging members $10', while the same letter applies the verification cost, about $2 a person, to non-members only. The verification exists, by the FAQ, so that the persons who certify that they are the authors 'are in fact who they say they are', and the announcement has the CEO speak of writers taking 'control of their professional identity'. What the certificate keeps is the author's own certification that a human wrote the text; the census record finds that the saved page does not say whether a certification may carry a pen name, and that a certified text is never shown to have been written without AI. On the archive's account of authorship under civil names, the metadata that lets a work be attributed to human authorship attaches to legal names, and the classifier of legitimate authorship reads legal-name attribution as its first signal. The archive distinguishes a pseudonym, whose function is traceable to the civil identity behind it, from a heteronym, whose function is attributable through the civil bearer without being reducible to that bearer, who stays accountable for custody, legal responsibility, rights and adjudication. On the census's reading the certificate binds the non-member's claim to an identity check, and the saved page leaves open whether it carries the name the author chose. By the licence the author represents and warrants that the work is Human Authored; a licensee who uses the mark on AI-generated text is in breach of the licence and liable for trademark infringement and, by the FAQ potentially and by the Guild's letter likely, for consumer fraud. The Guild states that it knows no truly reliable way to test a work for AI-generated material: the program is self-certification with enforcement, vets no manuscript before certifying, and may adopt detection software if a reliable one is found. Its stated measures against misuse are identity verification, a limit of ten new titles a year without permission, a registration number for each title, the public database and the fee. The census record accordingly holds the certificate to be no test of AI text and constitutes its function as self-certification under licence, covering the text. Jane Friedman, a Guild member with a marketing partnership with it, found certification on the honor system problematic because it takes the author's word and analyses no manuscript, and still held its market value negligible. The Guild answered that self-certification is standard in publishing and in legal agreements, that most authors are honest and concerned about liability, and that the program is not expected to break even. Friedman reported a hunch, from small presses' use of a detector, that works with some AI-generated or AI-assisted text approach 25 to 50 percent of nonfiction, and read the demand for certification as a sign of anti-AI conviction or of insecurity in the market. Others argued that the labelling runs backward, and one author asked whether books without the mark would be taken as created by AI; the Guild agrees that books with significant AI-generated content should be labelled, holds that consumers have a right to know, and its CEO calls the certification the next best solution absent a ruling that forces such labels. The database page answers the bookstore question for its own records: a lack of results means only that a work has not been registered as Human Authored, 'not that it is generated by AI'. Friedman's further concern, false accusations of AI use between authors, already a common insult, is the case the archive names the existence tax: before anyone talks about the work, its maker has to prove again that it exists, and exists as what it is. The archive keeps four questions apart, whether the maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and finds the tax levied when evidence on one is spent as an answer to another. On the census's reading the certificate answers a verdict of fakeness with the author's own certification. The archive finds the tax falling on the independent, the new, the unaccredited, the heteronymous and the small, and its remedy for a maker is a documentary layer dated, deposited and linked, against which an answer can be checked. An adequate answer, on its account, names the object at its own level, a person or a pen name among them, and shows its evidence; it holds a heteronym declared where a Sybil attack hides one actor behind many, its registry published with the orthonym, the roles and the dates. The mark is the words Human Authored in a circle around a human silhouette, issued in an updated form in March 2026; an author or publisher registers each work and agrees to the licence before using it. It may go on the front or back cover, typically a bottom corner of the back, on the copyright page with the registration number, which not every use need display, and in listings and marketing for the registered title, between a quarter of an inch and an inch across; violating the usage guidelines violates the licence. Its trademark status is stated two ways: the FAQ calls it a registered certification mark, while the announcement, Friedman and the Guild's own letter give a pending application with the US Patent and Trademark Office. Publishers Weekly gives its tagline as 'Certifying Human Creativity in an AI World'; the program page's line is 'Distinguish human creativity in an increasingly AI world'. The public database lists each certified title, searchable by title, author or registration number, the number usually printed on the copyright page, so that anyone can check a use of the mark and report misuse; it answers whether a named book is certified, and the census record ran no lookup in it. Beside it stand other certifications of human authorship: Created by Humans, from June 2024, which later partnered with the Guild and took its CEO as an adviser; Books by People in the United Kingdom, from 2025; the Society of Authors' scheme; and services such as Verify My Writing, which scores a manuscript for human content with a detector. Wikipedia has no article on the program: 'Human Authored' redirects to a section of the article on the Authors Guild, which gives the program page's definition, the fee as of 2026 and the open database, and cites Kit Eaton's comparison, in Inc. in October 2024, with food labelled 'organic'. The archive's packet Provenance Is What Authorship Must Endure grants the certification a legitimate function, protecting readers from deceptive synthetic substitution and keeping a market signal for AI-free literary labour, and calls the label 'a market-category signal, not a complete theory of authorship'. It finds in the certification a binary frame, AI-assisted work falling outside the human-authored category, and answers: 'Authorship is not a purity state. It is an accountability structure.' Its invariant places authorship in the accountable relation between writer, process and text, and its fourth position admits AI-mediated writing as authorship where provenance preserves the writer's directing and responsibility-bearing role, refusing the purism on which any generative AI participation destroys authorship. The packet opposes only the implication that AI-mediated authorship is impossible, holds that the two positions can coexist, and closes that the label matters, that the law is right to reject machine authorship, and that none of it is enough. It holds detection forensic and authorship moral and epistemic, and gives provenance the work of distinguishing authorship from slop; the Guild, for its part, leaves detection to software it has not found. The census reads the certificate as setting authorship's boundary at the human writing of a text and admitting machine participation only as minimal uses, so that where machine participation is constitutive of a work its definition leaves no certifiable place. The archive's own corpus declares the machine participation that boundary turns on: the packet counts its deposits as all produced through AI-mediated workflows, with declared provenance, and all authored, and a paper of the archive declares itself written with AI through the heteronymous voices that sign it. The archive argues that under a human-only policy enforced by a classifier the certified absence of machine mediation becomes the most machine-determined property of the text, and that a classifier introduced after an act gains standing over it without new evidence about the act; it disclaims any claim that a venue may not reserve space for human-composed work, and the Guild's program enforces by licence while its FAQ contemplates detection software. On the archive's account of civil names, the credentialed author need declare no substrate, the uncredentialed author who declares one is anomalous, and a function legible without civil-identity reduction looks to the regime like fraud. The heteronymy paper extends heteronymic organization to named machine-witness functions with their substrate and editorial chain declared, holds the operation not species-restricted, and leaves outside heteronymy machine assistance not organized as a declared witness role. Asked for the certification on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview gave, by the Capture Registry's reading, what it certifies, allows and excludes, its costs, the mark and the database, from five cards, three of them the Guild's. The registry finds the certificate composed at its grain, the requirements and the registration number among it, and the definition's minimal uses widened to outlining, indexing and brainstorming, with the text 'written entirely by a human'. It finds the member's identity given as verified on joining where the program page states a waiver; the FAQ card and Publishers Weekly state the verification on joining. The registry finds the census's question, which name the certificate carries, unreached, and the composition's close offering multi-author works as a next step, a matter the FAQ card answers.
